pages.title: What actually changed about search
pages.description: AI answer engines do not rank pages for a user to choose from. They read sources and produce one answer. That single structural difference is what makes AEO a different job from SEO.
pages.keywords: lesson Orientation
pages.body: The shift is from a list to a decision A search engine returns a list and lets the user decide. An answer engine reads a set of sources and makes the decision on the user's behalf, then presents the result as prose. The user often never sees the list at all. This is not a change in ranking mechanics. It is a change in what the surface is for. Optimizing for position on a list you are no longer shown is the wrong objective function. The question is no longer "where do we rank" but "when the engine composes an answer about our category, are we in it, is what it says about us true, and does it recommend us." Those are three separate questions with three separate failure modes, and most teams collapse them into one metric and then wonder why the metric does not move. Answer engines cite consensus, not authority The most common wrong intuition carried over from SEO is that a strong domain wins. Once a page is retrieved, answer engines are not primarily rewarding domain strength. They are assembling a picture from multiple sources and favouring what several independent sources agree on. That is why a brand can hold the top organic position for its own category term and still be absent from the AI answer for that same term. The page ranks. The claim is not corroborated anywhere else. The engine has one source saying it and no second source confirming it, so it composes an answer from the sources that do agree with each other. The practical consequence: a large part of AEO work happens off your own domain. Not because owned content stopped mattering — owned content is what converts the click and what an engine reads to learn your facts — but because a claim that exists only on your site reads to an engine as an assertion, not a finding. At the end of each lesson there is a Read next block pointing into our reference library. Those are the long-form pieces. This course is the spine; those are the depth. The budget, and the one way to waste it The free tier gives you three manual ChatGPT checks a month, one Deep Analysis, one Content Audit, ten tracked prompts, and one workspace. This course spends that budget on exactly one experiment: baseline, change, confirm. The way to waste it is to run a check early out of curiosity, before your prompt set is right. If you burn a run on a prompt set you are about to rewrite, your baseline and your follow-up are measuring different things and the comparison is meaningless. Do not run anything until Module 3 tells you to. This constraint is real, but it is also the lesson. Teams with unlimited runs remeasure until they see a number they like. A three-run budget forces you to decide in advance what you are testing — which is what a real experiment requires anyway. Why you cannot finish this in one sitting Modules 1 through 6 can be done in an afternoon. Module 7 cannot, because it asks you to remeasure after a content change, and a content change does not reach answer engines instantly. Depending on the engine, the source, and how often it is recrawled, that takes days to weeks. Quotas reset monthly, which fits this rhythm. Take your baseline and ship your change in month one; verify in month two. If that feels slow, that is accurate information about AEO rather than a limitation of the course.

pages.title: Why context comes before measurement
pages.description: You cannot grade an AI answer as right or wrong without a written statement of what is true. Corporate Context is that statement, and it has to exist before the first run.
pages.keywords: lesson Ground
pages.body: Accuracy needs a reference It is easy to measure whether an engine mentioned you. It is much harder, and much more valuable, to measure whether what it said was correct. That second measurement is impossible without a written source of truth to compare against. This is the reason context comes first in this course rather than as a later refinement. A baseline taken without a reference statement can only tell you presence. A baseline taken with one can tell you presence and accuracy, and accuracy is usually where the actionable problem is hiding. What belongs in it, and what does not Corporate Context is not marketing copy. It is the factual substrate: what the product does, who it is for, what it costs, what it does not do, how it differs from the named alternatives, and which claims you can substantiate. The instinct to write it persuasively is the main failure. Persuasive copy is full of unfalsifiable claims — "the leading platform," "trusted by teams everywhere" — and an unfalsifiable claim cannot be used to grade an answer. If an engine said it, you could not mark it right or wrong. Write things that could be checked. The second failure is silence. Whatever your context does not mention cannot be graded, so a gap in the document becomes a blind spot in every accuracy measurement that follows. If pricing is not in there, you will never learn that engines are quoting a price you retired two years ago. Include: what it is, who it serves, concrete capabilities, pricing structure, named alternatives and honest differences, substantiable proof points Include: the things you are commonly confused with — a same-name company, an adjacent category, a product you sunset Exclude: superlatives, unfalsifiable positioning, anything you would not want an engine to repeat verbatim It is organization-level, not per-workspace One practical detail that surprises people: Corporate Context is set at the organization level and shared across every workspace underneath it. pages.title: Writing your Corporate Context
pages.description: A working structure for the document, and the test for whether each line earns its place.
pages.keywords: lesson Ground
pages.body: A structure that works There is no required schema, but the documents that produce good grading tend to share a shape. Start with identity and disambiguation, then capability, then commercial facts, then the competitive frame, then proof. Disambiguation deserves more attention than it usually gets. If any company, product, or common phrase shares your name, say so explicitly and say what you are not. Engines conflate similar names constantly, and a single clarifying sentence in your context is the cheapest fix available for a whole class of wrong answers. Identity — legal name, product names, what category you are in, what you are commonly confused with Capability — what the product actually does, stated concretely enough to be checked Commercial — pricing structure, tiers, what is free, how someone starts Competitive — the alternatives buyers actually name, and where you genuinely differ Proof — claims you can substantiate, with the substantiation The test for every line For each sentence, ask: if an answer engine repeated this to a buyer, could I mark it true or false? If the answer is no, the sentence is positioning, not context. Move it to your website and take it out of here. The second test: is this still true? Context documents rot faster than anything else in marketing because pricing changes, tiers get renamed, features ship and get retired. A context document that says something you retired is worse than one that says nothing, because it will actively teach the wrong fact and you will grade answers against a standard that is itself wrong. Length is not the goal, coverage is A long document is not a good document. What matters is whether it covers the topics buyers actually ask about. The fastest way to find the gaps is to look at the questions in your own sales calls, then check whether your context answers each one. You will come back to this. After Module 5 you will have real evidence about which topics engines get wrong about you, and the first fix for

pages.title: Brand facts and the competitive set
pages.description: Naming your real competitors is a measurement decision, not a marketing one — and getting it wrong quietly corrupts every comparison you make afterwards.
pages.keywords: lesson Ground
pages.body: Name the competitors buyers name The competitive set you track should be the one buyers actually mention, not the one your positioning deck aspires to. These are frequently different, and the difference matters because share-of-voice against a set that does not reflect the real consideration set is a number that cannot inform any decision. The quickest way to get this right is to ask a few recent buyers what else they looked at, or read the alternatives your own sales calls surface. Then add anyone an answer engine names when asked about your category, even if you do not consider them a real competitor — if the engine names them to buyers, they are in your consideration set whether you like it or not. Brand facts versus Corporate Context Corporate Context is the narrative substrate. Brand facts are the discrete, checkable statements you want available for grounding — the specific numbers, dates, capabilities, and claims. Keep them separate in your head: context teaches an engine who you are, facts give it things it can quote. Facts can be extracted from documents and URLs and then curated, which is usually faster than writing them from scratch, but curate them properly — an extracted fact that is stale or out of context is a wrong answer waiting to be repeated.

pages.title: A prompt set is not a keyword list
pages.description: Keywords are fragments people type. Prompts are decisions people are trying to make. Porting one into the other is the most common way teams get an AEO programme wrong from day one.
pages.keywords: lesson Measure
pages.body: The unit of measurement changed In search, the unit is a query fragment — two or three words, stripped of intent, matched against a corpus. In AI answers, the unit is a question with a decision behind it: which tool should I use, is this vendor credible, what happens if I do this instead. If you export your keyword list and paste it in as prompts, you will measure something, but it will not be the thing that matters. "aeo tools" as a prompt produces a generic listing answer. "Which AEO tool should a five-person marketing team pick if they cannot afford Profound?" produces the answer a real buyer receives — and the two have different sources, different competitors named, and different implications for what you should do next. The four kinds of prompt worth tracking A prompt set that only asks one kind of question gives you a one-dimensional picture. Cover the decision journey instead. The recommendation prompts are the ones that hurt when you lose them, because they are the moment the engine picks someone. The accuracy prompts are the ones that hurt when you win them wrongly — being present in an answer that misdescribes you is worse than being absent. Category — what is this, how does it work, what should I know. You are competing with explainers here, not vendors. Comparison — X versus Y, alternatives to X. The competitive set becomes visible in these. Recommendation — what should I use, best tool for a situation. This is where the purchase decision happens. Brand — what is your company, is it any good, what does it cost. This is where accuracy problems surface. Ten is a real constraint, not a starter allowance Ten prompts is what the free tier tracks, and it is genuinely tight. But a focused ten beats a sprawling hundred for learning, because with ten you will actually read every answer, and reading the answers is where the insight is. Teams with large prompt sets frequently stop reading the responses and start watching only the aggregate score. That is how a prog

pages.title: Choosing your ten prompts
pages.description: A concrete allocation, the sourcing method, and the rule that keeps your baseline comparable to your follow-up.
pages.keywords: lesson Measure
pages.body: An allocation that balances A workable split across ten: three category, three comparison, two recommendation, two brand. That gives you enough of each type to notice a pattern, and it deliberately weights toward the top of the journey where most brands are weakest. Adjust for your situation. If you are in a category where buyers already know they need the thing, drop a category prompt and add a recommendation one. If you suspect an accuracy problem, take a second brand prompt. Where to source them The best prompts come from three places, in this order of quality. First, questions real buyers asked you — sales call notes, support tickets, the questions that come up in demos. These are unimpeachable because they actually happened. Second, what the engines themselves surface. Ask an answer engine a broad question about your category and read what follow-up questions it suggests or what sub-topics it volunteers. That is a direct read on how the engine has structured the space. Third, demand data — the aggregate of what people are asking AI in your industry. Useful for coverage, weaker for specificity, because a high-volume generic prompt often has less decision-weight than a low-volume specific one. The freeze rule Once you take your baseline, do not change the prompt set until after your verification run in Module 7. This is the rule that makes the whole experiment valid. If you edit a prompt between baseline and follow-up, you cannot attribute a change in the number to your content work, because the question itself changed. This sounds obvious and is violated constantly, usually with the excuse that the prompt was badly worded. If a prompt is badly worded, fix it now — before the baseline — and accept that anything you change afterwards is a new experiment, not a continuation of this one.

pages.title: Your first run: taking a baseline
pages.description: What a run actually does, what the first set of numbers means, and the discipline of writing down your prediction before you look.
pages.keywords: lesson Measure
pages.body: What a run is A run puts each of your prompts to the engine, captures the full response, and then parses it: was the brand mentioned, which sources were cited, which competitors appeared, how was the brand characterised. The value is not the score at the top — it is the corpus of actual answers underneath it. On the free tier a run covers ChatGPT. That is one engine of several, and the results will not generalise perfectly to Perplexity or Google's AI surfaces, which favour different sources. Know that limitation rather than forgetting it: your conclusions are about ChatGPT until you measure elsewhere. Write your prediction down first Before you trigger the run, write down what you expect. Which prompts do you think you will appear in? Which competitor do you expect to be named most? What do you think the engine will get wrong about you? This takes two minutes and it is the difference between learning something and confirming what you already believed. Without a written prediction, whatever you see will feel roughly like what you expected, because that is how memory works. With one, you get a genuine surprise, and the surprises are where the work is. Reading the first result honestly The first number will probably be lower than you hoped. That is normal and is not yet a finding — it is a starting coordinate. A baseline is not a grade. It is the thing you will subtract from later. Resist two temptations. The first is to immediately rerun because the result looked wrong; that spends a second unit of a three-unit budget on a sample you have no reason to distrust. The second is to start fixing things immediately. You have not diagnosed anything yet — Module 4 is where the answers get read properly, and acting before diagnosis is how teams ship changes that address a problem they do not have.

pages.title: Reading presence without over-reading it
pages.description: Presence, share of voice, and how a brand can be mentioned everywhere and recommended nowhere.
pages.keywords: lesson Read
pages.body: Three numbers that are not the same Presence is whether you appeared at all. Share of voice is how much of the named competitive set was you. Recommendation is whether the engine actually endorsed you rather than merely listing you. These decouple constantly. A brand can appear in nine of ten answers and be recommended in none, because it keeps being named in the roll-call of alternatives while a competitor is named as the choice. On a presence metric that looks like a win. Commercially it is a loss, and a loss you will not notice unless you look at recommendation separately. Aggregate scores hide the thing you need A single visibility score is useful for tracking direction over time and nearly useless for deciding what to do. The decision information lives in the per-prompt breakdown: which specific questions you lose, and to whom. Sort by the prompts where you are absent and read those responses first. That set is your actual work queue. A prompt where you are absent and a well-corroborated competitor is recommended is a different problem from one where the engine gave a generic answer naming nobody — the first is a competitive gap, the second is an unclaimed space, and they need opposite responses.

pages.title: Reading the citations
pages.description: The list of sources an engine cited is the most actionable artefact you have, because it names exactly which pages you would need to be on.
pages.keywords: lesson Read
pages.body: Citations are a map of what to influence When an engine composes an answer about your category, it draws on specific URLs. That list is not trivia. It is a directory of the pages that currently shape what buyers are told, and therefore the concrete targets for any off-domain work. Read them as a set, not individually. Look for the pages that recur across many prompts — those are the load-bearing sources in your category, and presence on one of them is worth more than presence on a dozen one-off mentions. Cited does not mean the page mentions you A subtle and important distinction: an engine can cite a page that has nothing to say about your brand. The citation tells you the engine used that page to answer the question, not that the page endorsed you. So a page cited on a prompt you lose is a target — being covered there could change the answer. A page cited on a prompt you win, which does mention you, is an asset — worth protecting and worth understanding, because whatever it says about you is currently working.

pages.title: The source layer: owned, editorial, community
pages.description: Different source types behave differently, respond to different work, and cannot substitute for each other.
pages.keywords: lesson Read
pages.body: Four layers, four different jobs Sort your cited domains into owned (yours), competitor, editorial (publications, analysts, reviewers), and community (forums, discussion sites, user-generated content). Each behaves differently and each is influenced by a different kind of work. Owned is the layer you control completely and the layer engines trust least on its own, because a claim on your own site is an assertion. Editorial is slow to move and heavily weighted. Community is fast, volatile, and frequently the largest single share of citations in a technical or software category — and it is also where the most brand-damaging misinformation lives. One engine-specific caveat: in August 2026 ChatGPT all but stopped citing Reddit, so on the ChatGPT-only free tier the community layer may look much smaller than it does on Google's AI surfaces or Perplexity. Owned content is not dismissed, it is misunderstood It is common to see the owned share of citations reported as a small percentage and concluded from that that owned content does not matter. That is a misreading. Any single domain holding a meaningful share of a category's citations is a strong position, because the denominator is every source on the open web. More importantly, the layers do different jobs in one funnel. Third-party sources are what make an engine willing to say your name. Your own pages are what the engine reads to get your facts right, and what converts the buyer who clicks through. Trying to substitute one for the other is how programmes end up either invisible or unable to convert the visibility they earned. Match the work to the layer The layer distribution in your citations tells you where the work is. If editorial dominates your category, your gap is a coverage and relationships problem. If community dominates, your gap is a participation problem, and the only ethical way in is to be genuinely useful in those communities rather than to plant mentions. If your own domain is absent even from prompts

pages.title: The three failure modes
pages.description: Not retrieved, retrieved but not cited, cited but not recommended. Almost every AEO problem is one of these, and treating them as one problem is why most fixes fail.
pages.keywords: lesson Diagnose
pages.body: Why one label is not enough "We are not visible in AI" is a symptom, not a diagnosis, and it covers three separate mechanical failures that happen at different stages and need opposite responses. Shipping a fix without knowing which one you have is guessing. The three are sequential. Retrieval has to succeed before citation is possible; citation has to happen before recommendation is on the table. Find the earliest stage that is failing and fix that, because fixing a later stage while an earlier one is broken changes nothing. Not retrieved — the engine never reached your content. Crawler access, rendering, or simply no content on the topic. Retrieved but not cited — the engine reached it and did not use it. Usually a corroboration or answer-shape problem. Cited but not recommended — the engine used you as a source and still endorsed someone else. Localising which one you have Not retrieved shows up as total absence — your domain appears nowhere in the citations, including on brand prompts where you should be the obvious source. Check crawler access first; content that requires JavaScript to render, or a robots configuration that excludes AI crawlers, produces exactly this pattern. Retrieved but not cited looks like your domain appearing occasionally but never on the prompts you care about. The content exists and is reachable but is not what the engine wants for that question — usually because it does not answer the question in a directly extractable form, or because nothing else on the web corroborates the claim. Cited but not recommended is the most advanced problem and the most commercially frustrating. Your content is good enough to inform the answer and something else is winning the endorsement — typically because the competitor has independent corroboration you lack.

pages.title: Running a Deep Analysis
pages.description: You have one on the free tier. Spend it on the prompt that matters most, not the one that annoys you most.
pages.keywords: lesson Diagnose
pages.body: What it adds over reading the response Reading responses tells you what happened. A Deep Analysis works on why — examining the answer against your context and the cited sources to produce reasoning about the gap and specific recommendations rather than a score. The output is only as good as the Corporate Context underneath it. This is where the work in Module 2 pays off, and where a thin context document produces disappointingly generic recommendations. If the analysis comes back vague, the usual cause is that your context did not give it enough to reason with. Choosing which prompt to spend it on You have one. The instinct is to spend it on the answer that is most wrong about you, because that one is irritating. Usually the better choice is the prompt with the most commercial weight where you are absent — a recommendation prompt in your core category. Ask which prompt, if the answer changed, would most change the pipeline. Spend the analysis there.

pages.title: Auditing one page
pages.description: The page-level view: whether a specific URL is answer-ready, and what recovering the lost points actually requires.
pages.keywords: lesson Diagnose
pages.body: Page-level readiness is a separate question Prompt-level measurement tells you what engines say about your category. A content audit asks a narrower question about one URL: is this page structured so an engine can extract an answer from it, and is it credible enough to be worth citing. These are graded across content quality, credibility, technical readability, and discoverability. The credibility weighting surprises people — sourced statistics, external citations, and clear authorship carry real weight, which is the page-level expression of the consensus principle from Module 1. Choosing the URL You have one audit. Spend it on the page that should be winning a prompt you are losing — not your homepage, which is rarely the page an engine wants for a specific question. If your Deep Analysis pointed at a content gap, the right URL is the page that ought to cover that gap. If no such page exists, that is itself the finding, and Module 6 becomes about creating it rather than fixing something. Read the recoverable points, not the score The score is a summary. The useful part is the itemised list of what is missing and how many points each would recover, because that is a ranked work list with effort implied. Work top-down and be honest about which items you can substantiate. An audit may note that sourced statistics would help; inventing a statistic to satisfy it is worse than leaving the points on the table, because a fabricated fact is exactly what accuracy monitoring exists to catch.

pages.title: When presence is not the problem
pages.description: Two failure states that a presence metric will never show you: the engine describes you wrongly, or describes you correctly and still picks someone else.
pages.keywords: lesson Diagnose
pages.body: Being present and wrong An answer that mentions you and misdescribes you is worse than one that omits you, because it actively teaches a buyer something false and it does so with the engine's authority behind it. Presence metrics score this as a win. Grading requires the reference document from Module 2, which is why context came first. The frequent finding is not dramatic hallucination but quiet staleness — a retired price, a feature you sunset, a positioning you moved away from two years ago. The web still says it, so the engine still says it. Note the coverage limit: anything your context is silent about cannot be graded. If accuracy grading comes back clean, check whether that means you are accurate or whether it means your context does not cover the topics where you are wrong. Being present, correct, and still not chosen The hardest state. The engine has your facts right, cites your page, and recommends a competitor anyway. There is nothing to correct. This is almost always corroboration. The competitor's claim is echoed across independent sources; yours exists on your own site and nowhere else. The engine is doing what Module 1 described — favouring what several sources agree on — and the fix is not a better page. It is a third-party source that says the same thing. That is slower and less controllable than editing your own content, which is why teams avoid diagnosing it correctly and ship another landing page instead. If you are in this state, Module 6 has to be about the source layer, not about your own site.

pages.title: Why you ship exactly one change
pages.description: Shipping five changes at once feels productive and destroys your ability to learn anything from the result.
pages.keywords: lesson Act
pages.body: Attribution requires restraint If you fix the page, publish two new articles, get a review site listing, and update your schema in the same week, and the number moves, you have learned that something worked. You have not learned what, so you cannot do it again on purpose. One change per cycle is slower per week and much faster per lesson learned. After three cycles the team that changed one thing at a time knows three things. The team that changed fifteen things knows that their numbers went up. This is genuinely hard to hold to under pressure to show activity. The defence is to be explicit that the cycle is an experiment with a stated hypothesis, not a sprint of content output. Write the hypothesis before you ship State it in one sentence: because the engine is failing at [mode], I am changing [thing], and I expect [specific prompt] to show [specific movement] by [date]. A hypothesis that cannot fail is not one. "This will improve our AI visibility" is unfalsifiable. "This should make us appear in the answer to prompt 4, which we currently lose to a named competitor" can be checked, and can be wrong, which is what makes it worth testing. Write down the date you will remeasure, and make it at least two weeks out.

pages.title: Fixing a page so an engine can use it
pages.description: For retrieval and citation failures, what actually changes an outcome — and the shortcuts that produce nothing.
pages.keywords: lesson Act
pages.body: Answer the question in an extractable form The most reliable page-level improvement is unglamorous: state the direct answer to the question, early, in plain declarative sentences, before the context and the narrative. Engines extract. A page that buries its answer under four hundred words of preamble is harder to extract from than one that answers in the first paragraph and then elaborates. This is not about writing shallowly; elaborate all you want afterwards. It is about not making the extractable claim conditional on reading the whole piece. Define your terms explicitly, use headings that match how the question is actually asked, and put the specific claim, number, or comparison in prose rather than only in an image or a chart. Credibility carries real weight Sourced statistics, outbound citations to primary sources, clear authorship, and a visible date all contribute. This is the page-level version of the consensus principle: a page that shows its work reads as more citable than one that asserts. The constraint is honesty. Do not manufacture a statistic to satisfy a checklist, do not invent a review rating, do not add schema describing things that are not on the page. Structured data that does not match the content is a well-known way to get ignored, and a fabricated fact is the thing accuracy monitoring exists to catch. What structured data does and does not do Schema helps a machine parse what a page is and how its parts relate. It does not make a page authoritative, and it will not rescue content that has nothing to say. Treat it as removing friction rather than adding weight. Match the schema type to the actual content, keep it complete, and make sure the page is readable without JavaScript — a page whose content only exists after client-side rendering is a retrieval failure waiting to be diagnosed.

pages.title: When the fix is off your own site
pages.description: For corroboration failures, the work is on someone else's domain — which changes the timeline, the tactics, and the ethics.
pages.keywords: lesson Act
pages.body: You cannot edit your way out of a corroboration gap If you are cited, accurate, and still not recommended, the missing ingredient is an independent source that says what you say. No amount of work on your own site produces that. The targets are already in your data. Module 4 asked you to identify the source URLs that recur across the prompts you lose. Those are not abstract; they are the specific pages where being covered would change the answer. Match the tactic to the layer Editorial coverage responds to being genuinely newsworthy or genuinely useful to that publication's audience — a real finding, a dataset, a point of view worth quoting. It is slow and it does not respond to volume. Review and directory listings are the most mechanical option and often underrated, because they are structured, frequently recrawled, and explicitly comparative. Community sources are the fastest-moving and the most dangerous to approach cynically. The only durable strategy is to be a useful participant. Astroturfing is detectable by humans and increasingly by platforms, and it converts a citation opportunity into a reputational liability. Expect a slower clock Off-domain work has a longer lag than a page edit. Publication, then crawl, then incorporation into what engines draw on. If your change this cycle is off-domain, extend your remeasurement date accordingly rather than concluding it failed at two weeks. That is a real cost, and it is why diagnosing correctly matters. Spending a slow cycle on corroboration when your actual problem was crawler access is an expensive mistake.

pages.title: Why one run proves nothing
pages.description: Answer engines are non-deterministic. Understanding what that does to your evidence is the core skill this course exists to teach.
pages.keywords: lesson Verify
pages.body: The number moves on its own Ask the same prompt twice with nothing changed and you can get different sources, a different set of competitors named, and sometimes a different recommendation. The output is a draw from a distribution. This means your measurement has natural variance independent of anything you do. If you observe a change after shipping something, part of that change is your work and part is the distribution. With a single before-and-after observation you cannot tell which part is which — and the honest answer is often that you cannot tell at all. How this goes wrong in practice The failure is not usually dishonesty, it is asymmetric attention. A team ships a change, sees the number rise, and stops looking. The same team ships a change, sees the number fall, and concludes the measurement is noisy. Both readings might be right, but applying them selectively guarantees the wrong conclusion. The defence is deciding in advance. Before you remeasure, write down what movement you would count as success and what you would count as failure. Then hold yourself to it even when you dislike the answer. Some prompts are noisier than others Variance is not uniform. Some questions have a settled answer that the engines return consistently; others are contested, with the named set shifting between draws. This distinction is directly useful. A settled prompt where you lose is expensive to move but the win is durable. A contested prompt is cheaper to move and less stable — and it is also where an opening still exists, because the consensus has not formed yet. Knowing which of your prompts are which tells you where effort compounds.

pages.title: Your second run
pages.description: Remeasure against a frozen prompt set, and read the per-prompt movement rather than the headline.
pages.keywords: lesson Verify
pages.body: Conditions for a valid comparison Three things must be true. The prompt set is unchanged from the baseline. Enough time has passed for the change to propagate — at least two weeks for a page edit, longer for anything off-domain. And you have written down in advance what would count as success. If any is false, run anyway if you like, but be clear that you are collecting an observation rather than testing a hypothesis. Read the prompt you targeted first Your hypothesis named a specific prompt. Look at that one before the aggregate, because the aggregate blends the prompt you targeted with nine you did not touch, and that blend can easily hide or manufacture the effect. Then read the actual response, not just whether the flag flipped. Sometimes the informative result is that you are now cited but still not recommended — which is not failure, it is progress to the next failure mode, and it tells you what the following cycle is about.

pages.title: Signal or noise: the third run
pages.description: The run most teams never take, and the only one that tells you whether the second one meant anything.
pages.keywords: lesson Verify
pages.body: What the third run is for The second run gives you one post-change observation. The third gives you a second one, with nothing changed in between — which lets you see how much the number moves on its own. If run three sits close to run two and both are clearly different from the baseline, you have a result worth acting on. If run three swings back toward the baseline, what you saw in run two was substantially variance, and the honest conclusion is that the change did not demonstrably work. This is the run that gets skipped, because by run two the team already has the story it wants. Taking it is the single practice that most separates an AEO programme that compounds from one that accumulates unverified folklore. Recording the outcome honestly Write down which of three things happened: the change worked, it did not, or the result was inconclusive. Inconclusive is a legitimate and common outcome, and recording it as such is what stops it from being remembered as a success six months later. Record the effect size too, not just the direction. A change that moved one prompt from absent to mentioned is a different fact from one that moved you from mentioned to recommended across four prompts, and treating them as the same is how a tactic gets over-generalised. What to do with each outcome If it worked: do the same class of change on the next-highest-value gap. You have evidence about your specific category, which is worth more than any generic best practice. If it did not: revisit the diagnosis rather than the tactic. The usual cause is a correct fix applied to the wrong failure mode. If it was inconclusive: either the effect is real but smaller than your variance, or there is no effect. Both point to the same next step — pick a higher-leverage change rather than repeating this one harder.

pages.title: Turning this into an operating cadence
pages.description: What the loop looks like when it runs every month, what to report, and what to stop doing.
pages.keywords: lesson Verify
pages.body: The cycle, repeated You have now run the loop once. The practice is that same loop on a monthly cadence: remeasure, diagnose the largest remaining gap, ship one change matched to its failure mode, verify, record. The prompt set should stay stable for several cycles so movement stays comparable, then be revised deliberately rather than continuously — when your category shifts or when a prompt has been settled in your favour long enough to stop being informative. Do not delete prompts that show zero presence. A prompt you have never won is where the opportunity is; deleting it only improves the average. What to report upward Report the experiment, not the dashboard. What did we believe, what did we change, what happened, what do we now know that we did not know last month. That framing survives contact with a sceptical executive far better than a visibility score, because it is falsifiable and it accumulates. It also protects you when a month produces an inconclusive result — you still learned something, and you have the record to prove the process is working even when the number did not move. Connect it to the commercial question when you can. Presence on a recommendation prompt in your core category is worth more than presence on a category-definition prompt, and saying so keeps the conversation about pipeline rather than about a number. What to stop doing Stop reading single answers as evidence. Stop shipping bundles of changes and attributing the result to whichever one you liked best. Stop reporting the aggregate score as the outcome. Stop deleting the prompts you lose. And stop treating advice — including everything in this course — as true without testing it in your own category. The point of building a measurement loop is that you no longer have to take anyone's word for it, including ours.
